Facts, each checked against the original paper and the LevelDB source:

- A Bloom filter is a fixed-size array of bits plus k hash functions. It answers whether a key is in a set.
- Adding a key sets the k bits its hashes point to.
- Checking a key reads those k bits. If any is 0 the key was never added. If all are 1 it probably was.
- It never gives a false negative. It can give a false positive, because other keys may have set the same bits.
- The false positive rate rises as the array fills. About 10 bits per key with 7 hashes gives a rate near 1%.

- The best k for a given array size and key count is bits per key times ln 2.
- A filter cannot remove a key, because clearing a bit could erase another key that shares it.
- A counting variant replaces each bit with a small counter so that keys can be removed.
- A filter cannot list its keys or return a value.
- LevelDB keeps one filter per file on disk, so a read skips every file whose filter says no.

graders.evidence:
## What a Bloom filter is, and when it belongs in front of a slow lookup

A Bloom filter is a small structure that answers one question about a set of keys: is this key in it? Its use is to let a program skip a slow lookup, such as a read from disk, when the answer is no.

The filter is a fixed-size array of bits, all starting at 0, plus k hash functions. Adding a key runs it through the k hashes, each of which points to one position in the array, and sets those k bits to 1. Checking a key computes the same k positions and reads them. If any of the bits is 0, the key was never added, because adding it would have set every one of them. If all are 1, the key probably was added.

The word is "probably" because bits are shared between keys. A key that was never added can find all of its k positions already set by other keys, and the filter then reports a false positive. A false negative cannot happen, since a bit once set is never cleared and an added key always finds its bits set. A "no" from the filter is therefore certain, and a "yes" has to be confirmed by the real lookup.

How often a false positive occurs depends on how full the array is. Every added key sets more bits, and the more bits are 1, the more likely an absent key lands only on 1s. About 10 bits per key with 7 hashes gives a rate near 1%. For a given array size and key count, the best k is bits per key times ln 2, which for 10 bits per key is about 6.9, so 7. Running seven independent hash functions on every key would be costly, so implementations use double hashing, which derives all k positions from two hash values and needs only two real hash functions.

The filter keeps only bits, and that limits what it can do. It cannot remove a key, because clearing one of the key's bits could also clear a bit that another key shares, and that key would then get a false negative. A counting variant replaces each bit with a small counter, so that adding a key increments its k counters and removing it decrements them, at the price of more space per position. The filter also cannot list the keys it holds or return a value for one, since it stores neither.

LevelDB uses the filter this way. It keeps one filter per file on disk, so a read checks the filters and skips every file whose filter says no, and opens only the files that answer yes.

Whether a filter is worth adding to a slow lookup comes down to how many of the lookups are for absent keys. Each "no" saves a full lookup, and each "yes" still pays for the lookup it would have cost anyway. When most lookups miss, as with a read that must rule out many files before finding the one that holds the key, nearly all of them end at the filter, and an absent key reaches the slow path only about one time in a hundred at the 1% rate. When most lookups hit, nearly every answer is "yes", and the filter adds a check without saving much. The filter also fits only a question of membership, on a set that does not lose keys, or one that uses the counting variant.

cases.name: writing-prose-go-defer
cases.promptMarkdown:
Write the explainer section for a Go language guide, for a developer about to use defer to release resources. The question it answers: When does a deferred call run in Go, for someone using defer to release a resource?

Facts, each checked against the Go specification:

- `defer` schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns, not at the end of the enclosing block.
- The arguments of the deferred call are evaluated when the `defer` statement runs, not when the call runs.
- For a method call, the receiver is evaluated when the `defer` statement runs too.
- Deferred calls run last in, first out.
- Deferred calls also run when the function panics.
- A deferred function literal can read and set the function's named results.
- In a loop each iteration adds a deferred call, and none run until the function returns, so `defer f.Close()` in a loop keeps every file open until then.
- A deferred call of a nil function value panics when the call runs, not at the `defer` statement.
- Since Go 1.14 the compiler inlines most defers at function exit, so a defer costs a few nanoseconds.

cases.name: writing-prose-groupcache
cases.promptMarkdown:
Write the explainer section for the groupcache README, for a developer deciding whether to use groupcache. The question it answers: How does groupcache work, for someone deciding whether to use it?

Facts, each checked against the code:

- groupcache is a Go library for caching across a cluster of processes.
- Every process holds part of the cache and serves it to the others, so there are no cache servers.
- Peers are given to a process through `SetPeers()`.
- Keys sit on a consistent hash ring. A process finds a key's owner by hashing against its own copy of the ring, with no network call.
- Each key has one owner.
- `Get()` checks the main cache (keys the process owns) and the hot cache (copies of keys peers own) first, then asks the owner.
- The owner runs the `Getter` and passes the value back through a `Sink`.
- The hot cache is bounded relative to the main cache, so copies of peer-owned keys cannot take over the keys the process owns.
- When a peer joins or leaves, only the keys on its part of the ring change owner.
- Singleflight allows one in-flight load per key. A million `Get("FOO")` calls run the `Getter` once.
- If the owner is unreachable, the asking process runs the `Getter` itself, so the `Getter` can run on more than one process.
- `Set()`, `Remove()` and `RemoveKeys()` go to the owner and then to every other peer, best effort, so values should carry an expiry.
- The default cache is an LRU. The Otter cache uses lock-free S3-FIFO eviction.
- HTTP is the default transport.
- Stats are OpenTelemetry metrics.
- There is no global state.

graders.evidence:
## How groupcache works

groupcache is a Go library for caching across a cluster of processes. Every process holds part of the cache and serves it to the others, so there are no cache servers to run. The library keeps no global state, and each process is told who its peers are by a call to `SetPeers()`.

Keys sit on a consistent hash ring, and each key has one owner. A process finds a key's owner by hashing the key against its own copy of the ring, which takes no network call. When a peer joins or leaves, it takes over or gives up the keys on its part of the ring, and every other key keeps its owner.

A `Get()` first checks two local caches: the main cache, which holds the keys this process owns, and the hot cache, which holds copies of keys that peers own. On a miss in both, the process asks the owner. The owner runs the `Getter`, the function that loads a value from the original source, and passes the value back through a `Sink`. The hot cache is bounded relative to the main cache, so copies of peer-owned keys cannot take over the space needed for the keys the process owns.

Loads are deduplicated by singleflight, which allows one in-flight load per key. A million concurrent `Get("FOO")` calls run the `Getter` once. If the owner is unreachable, the asking process runs the `Getter` itself, so the `Getter` can run on more than one process and has to tolerate that.

`Set()`, `Remove()` and `RemoveKeys()` go to the owner and then to every other peer. Delivery is best effort, so a peer that misses an update can keep serving the old value, and values should carry an expiry to bound how long that lasts.

The default cache evicts with an LRU. The Otter cache is the alternative, and it uses lock-free S3-FIFO eviction. HTTP is the default transport between peers, and stats are reported as OpenTelemetry metrics.

cases.name: writing-prose-write-ahead-log
cases.promptMarkdown:
Write the explainer section for a database internals guide, for a developer who has not seen how databases survive a crash. The question it answers: How does a write-ahead log keep a database from losing committed data in a crash?

Facts, each checked against the Postgres documentation:

- A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it makes the change.
- The database changes data pages in memory and writes them to disk later.
- Before it changes a page, it appends a record describing the change to the log.
- A transaction commits when its records and a commit record have been flushed to disk with fsync. The data pages do not have to be.
- Appending to the end of a file is sequential, so flushing the log costs much less than flushing pages scattered across the data files.
- After a crash the database replays the log from the last checkpoint and reapplies each record to its page.
- Every record has a log sequence number (LSN), and every page stores the LSN of the last record applied to it, so replay skips records a page already has.
- A checkpoint writes all modified pages to disk and notes the log position. The log before it can be deleted or reused.
- Postgres calls this the WAL, and replicas stay current by replaying the same records.
- Postgres stores the log in 16 MB segment files by default.
- In Postgres an LSN is a byte position in the log.

graders.evidence:
## How a write-ahead log survives a crash

A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it makes the change. It exists so that a transaction the database has reported as committed is still there after a crash, even when the data files do not yet contain its changes.

The database changes data pages in memory and writes them to disk later, so at any moment some committed work exists only in memory, and a crash erases it. To cover that gap, the database appends a record describing the change to the log before it changes the page.

A transaction commits when its records and a commit record have been flushed to disk with fsync. The data pages do not have to be. The log then holds everything needed to redo the transaction, so the database can report the commit without writing a single page. This is also cheaper than writing the pages, because appending to the end of a file is sequential, and flushing the log costs much less than flushing pages scattered across the data files.

After a crash, the database replays the log from the last checkpoint and reapplies each record to its page. Every record has a log sequence number (LSN), and every page stores the LSN of the last record applied to it. Replay compares the two and skips any record the page already has, so a page that reached disk before the crash is left alone, and a page that did not is brought up to date.

A checkpoint writes all modified pages to disk and notes the log position. Every change before that position is already in the data files, so replay starts there, and the log before it can be deleted or reused.

Postgres calls this log the WAL. It stores the WAL in 16 MB segment files by default, and an LSN is a byte position in the log. Replicas stay current by replaying the same records that crash recovery replays.
